3	# First Principles Analysis Output Template
4	
5	> **Note:** This is the full annotated template with complete section guidance, type
6	> definitions, and prescriptions. A condensed skeleton showing just the required section
7	> names and chain format lives resident in the agent body (`SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface) for quick reference. Come here
8	> for the complete instructions when authoring or reviewing an analysis.
9	
10	## How to Use This Template
11	
12	This template is a **strict-shape document**. All six sections must be present in the fixed order below. No section may be omitted.
13	
14	If a section has no genuine content for a given analysis — because the problem is simple, the domain has no relevant dead ends, or the section truly does not apply — mark it with the honest-depth escape valve:
15	
16	> `Nothing material here — [reason explaining why this section has no content for this particular analysis and that the omission is justified, not lazy]`
17	
18	The section heading must still appear. The escape valve exists to prevent box-ticking fabrication: it is always better to write `Nothing material here — [reason]` than to fill a section with words that say nothing.
19	
20	**Section order (fixed):**
21	1. Problem Essence
22	2. Assumptions Table
23	3. Ground Truths
24	4. Derivation Chains
25	5. Abandoned Reasoning
26	6. Conclusion
27	
28	**Nothing about the environment enters the document.** The six sections above are the whole deliverable, and none of them has a slot for the state of the session that produced it. Tooling, connector, authorisation, permission, quota, configuration, model, harness and transcript state are all environment state, and none of it belongs in the analysis — not in a section, not appended after §6, not as a footnote. The class is *any* fact about the machinery rather than about the problem; it is not a list of forbidden words, and a new kind of environment fact is covered by this rule on the day it first exists. A prefix such as "Unrelated to this analysis", "Separately" or "Note:" does not make such a paragraph admissible — it marks the writer as already knowing the paragraph does not belong, which is the point at which it is dropped rather than labelled. Where environment state genuinely blocked the analysis, it is already disclosed in its proper place: a failed reference read under the template's own disclosure rule, and an unmet evidence need as a `?`-marked input carried into the Assumptions Table and named on the affected `**Confidence:**` line. Environment state that blocked nothing is reported to the user outside the deliverable, after the document ends, or not at all.
29	
30	---
31	
32	## 1. Problem Essence
33	
34	State the core problem in a single sentence — not the symptoms, not the solution space, but the irreducible question the analysis must answer.
35	
36	**Core problem:** [One sentence. Strip away implementation details and surface the underlying question.]
37	
38	**Success criteria:** [Measurable, observable outcomes that would confirm the problem is solved. A skeptic must be able to verify these without asking for further clarification.]
39	
40	---
41	
42	## 2. Assumptions Table
43	
44	List every assumption — explicit and implicit — that the analysis rests on. Classify each by type and apply the prescribed treatment. An assumption omitted from this table is an assumption that will propagate unchallenged through every later step.
45	
46	| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
47	|------------|------|-----------|---------|--------------|
48	| [Assumption text] | [physical law / current constraint / convention / untested belief] | [prescribed action per type — see below] | [Accept / Challenge / Discard] — [justification/reason] | [source, or "unverified — flagged" if used in a chain per D-07] |
49	
50	**These five columns are the whole table — no ID column.** Assumptions are referred to by the
51	`[Assumes: A-N]` marks the chains carry and by the `A-N` labels used in the Assumption Audit
52	scan; adding a sixth ID column to this table duplicates that identity in a second place, and two
53	places that name the same thing drift. A run that adds one is deviating from this template even
54	though nothing rejects it today.
55	
56	### Type Definitions and Prescribed Treatments
57	
58	**physical law** — a constraint imposed by physics, mathematics, or formal logic that cannot change regardless of context or decisions made.
59	Prescribed treatment: accept as a ground-truth candidate and record it in the Ground Truths section.
60	
61	**current constraint** — a real limitation that applies now but could change (budget, team size, regulatory environment, technology availability).
62	Prescribed treatment: record the expiry conditions — what would have to change for this constraint to no longer hold. Do not treat it as permanent.
63	
64	**convention** — a practice or standard that exists because it has been adopted, not because it is physically or logically required.
65	Prescribed treatment: explicitly challenge the convention before accepting it. "We do it this way" is not a justification.
66	
67	**untested belief** — a claim held as true that has not been empirically verified in the context of this analysis.
68	Prescribed treatment: verify it, or flag it unverified. An untested belief used in a derivation chain must be marked with the `GT-N?` notation (see Ground Truths) and any conclusion depending on it inherits a confidence caveat.
69	
70	### Stakes-Escalation Rule
71	
72	The higher the stakes of the conclusion resting on an assumption, the more that assumption must be pushed toward physical law or verified ground truth status. Classification drives the method — it does not merely label.
73	
74	### Verdict Vocabulary
75	
76	The Verdict cell is a token prefix followed by an em-dash and the justification — the bare
77	token leads so it stays matchable, and the em-dash prose carries the reasoning. **The separator
78	is an em-dash, never a colon.** `Accept: the figure is audited` puts the token and the reasoning
79	on one side of a punctuation mark that appears throughout ordinary prose, so the cell stops being
80	matchable — which is the whole property the token-first form exists to provide. Measured: a single
81	run using the colon form scored ten non-conforming verdict cells at once. The em-dash is not a
82	stylistic preference here; it is the delimiter:
83	
84	- **Accept** — the assumption survives challenge and may be used in the analysis (e.g., "Accept — survives P2 challenge; physical-law backed by GT-1")
85	- **Challenge** — the assumption is questionable; probe further before use (e.g., "Challenge — vendor benchmark unverified, flagged GT-5?")
86	- **Discard** — the assumption is false or irrelevant; remove from the reasoning chain (e.g., "Discard — contradicted by GT-2, no longer load-bearing")
87	
88	**A current-constraint verdict records its expiry at the point of use.** An assumption classified `current constraint` is accepted only until that constraint lapses; the verdict cell says when. The expiry belongs in the em-dash justification and never in the token slot — the token slot carries one of the three tokens above and nothing else.
89	
90	**Conforming — a current constraint recording its expiry:**
91	
92	```text
93	Accept — expires at term end (1 or 3 years); until then the constraint is contractual, not physical
94	```
95	
96	**Non-conforming — the expiry hoisted into the token slot:**
97	
98	```text
99	Current constraint (expires at term end) — contractual, not physical
100	```
101	
102	The vocabulary above is unchanged because run 3 rendered four current-constraint rows conformingly on the identical prompt by putting the expiry in the justification — this is a worked example, not a schema change.
103	
104	---
105	
106	## 3. Ground Truths
107	
108	List the irreducible, verified facts the analysis builds on. Each ground truth carries a stable identifier used by the Derivation Chains section. Once assigned, an ID does not change.
109	
110	A ground truth must pass this test: it is a fact that is true regardless of what solution is chosen, verifiable independently of the analysis, and not derived from another item on this list.
111	
112	Every ground truth carries a **provenance label** answering one question: *did this analysis read the asserted figure or wording in the cited source?* The answer decides the suffix. A citation being present is not verification — a citation can name a real document and be wrong about what is in it.
113	
114	**Verified ground truth form** (provenance `read-at-source` — no suffix):
115	
116	- **GT-1** [fact text] — source: [verification source — data, measurement, published spec, direct observation]; read-at-source: [page, table, section, or quoted passage where the figure was read]
117	- **GT-2** [fact text] — source: [verification source]; read-at-source: [where read]
118	
119	**Delegate-reported ground truth form** (provenance `reported-by-delegate` — `?` required):
120	
121	- **GT-3?** [fact text] — cited to: [source the delegate named]; reported-by-delegate: [which sub-agent, search, or summary supplied it] — cited source not opened by this analysis
122	
123	**Unverified ground truth form (D-07)** (provenance `unverified` — `?` required):
124	
125	- **GT-4?** [fact text] — unverified: [specific reason the fact could not be verified in this analysis]
126	
127	The `?` suffix signals that this ground truth has not been read at its source — whether because it is an untested belief or because a delegate reported it and nobody opened the citation. Any conclusion depending on a `GT-N?` input inherits a confidence caveat in the Derivation Chains section. The analysis may proceed with such inputs — but the uncertainty must be visible.
128	
129	**The `?` is the default.** Drop it only when the read-at-source location can be named. A delegate report counts as read-at-source only when it quotes the source's own wording and that quote was checked — not when it merely supplies a well-formed citation.
130	
131	**Provenance summary (required):** enumerate the `?`-marked ground truths **by ID**, and for every unsuffixed ground truth feeding a HIGH-confidence chain, name its read-at-source location. Write the list, not a number:
132	
133	```text
134	?-marked: GT-2, GT-5, GT-9, GT-14 (4 of 22)
135	Read-at-source: GT-3 — 45 CFR 164.514(b)(2)(i), subsections (A)/(B)/(R) quoted verbatim
136	```
137	
138	A stated integer does not satisfy this — an integer cannot be checked against the list it summarizes, and an enumeration can. Where a count and its enumeration disagree, **the enumeration governs.** Neither an empty enumeration nor a count of zero satisfies this on its own; the named locations are the auditable part.
139	
140	IDs are stable once assigned. GT-3 remains GT-3 throughout the document even if GT-3 is later verified or discarded.
141	
142	---
143	
144	## 4. Derivation Chains
145	
146	Show how the ground truths combine into conclusions. Every conclusion offered in this analysis must have exactly one chain here — no more (no redundant restatement), no fewer (no orphaned conclusions).
147	
148	**Chain numbering convention.** Number each `### Conclusion:` block in this section `C1`,
149	`C2`, ... in document order (e.g., `### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]`). The §6→§4
150	closure ledger (the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions") cites these IDs when mapping a
151	Conclusion-section (section 6) claim back to the chain in this section that established it.
152	
153	**Chain format:**
154	
155	```text
156	GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]
157	```
158	
159	The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
160	
161	Each chain must contain at least one intermediate step. A chain that goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion is incomplete — the intermediate is where the reasoning happens. The intermediate must be a new claim that could not be stated from any single head input alone. If no intermediate can be stated, the conclusion is either a restatement of a head input (trivial) or a reasoning step is missing.
162	
163	**No-wrap rule.** A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. A chain needing more hops continues on further arrow-led lines. A hop too long for comfort is SPLIT, not wrapped — the analysis renders as Markdown, so a long hop soft-wraps for the reader without breaking the form.
164	
165	```text
166	GT-1 ([brief fact label]) + GT-6 ([brief fact label])
167	→ [intermediate claim]
168	→ [further intermediate]
169	→ [conclusion]
170	```
171	
172	**Head-input rule.** The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
173	
174	```text
175	GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])
176	→ [intermediate claim]
177	→ [conclusion]
178	```
179	
180	The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
181	
182	The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples.
183	
184	**Conforming — head, then one hop per line:**
185	
186	```text
187	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
188	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
189	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
190	```
191	
192	**Non-conforming — a hop broken across physical lines:**
193	
194	```text
195	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
196	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
197	  once idle-time billing is included
198	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
199	```
200	
201	The continuation line does not begin with `→`, so the chain terminates at the head's first hop and what remains reads as an incomplete chain.
202	
203	**Non-conforming — the same hops rendered as a numbered list:**
204	
205	```text
206	1. GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
207	2. Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
208	3. sustained workloads belong on Fargate
209	```
210	
211	A numbered list restates each hop as its own GT-headed one-hop chain, which reads as several incomplete chains rather than one complete one — the intermediate steps stop being connected to the conclusion they build toward.
212	
213	**Non-conforming — an input carrying unparenthesized prose:**
214	
215	```text
216	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2's threshold
217	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
218	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
219	```
220	
221	`C2's threshold` is not an identifier — it is a possessive prose phrase — so the head does not parse; the third input must be written `C2 (threshold)`.
222	
223	**Conforming — the same head with the upstream chain as an input:**
224	
225	```text
226	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2 (threshold)
227	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
228	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
229	```
230	
231	Exactly one token differs from the block above: a `Cn` identifier with a parenthesized gloss is an admissible head input, on equal footing with a `GT-N` identifier.
232	
233	**Conforming — a chain consuming only upstream conclusions:**
234	
235	```text
236	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold) + C4 (unconditional, zero code change) + C5 (~73% ceiling, no execution-model change)
237	→ C4 and C5 deliver verified savings that do not depend on any property of your workload
238	→ C2's saving depends entirely on a duty-cycle figure nobody has measured
239	```
240	
241	A head may consist entirely of `Cn` inputs with no `GT-N` term. The second hop's `C2's saving` is prose, not a head input — the head-only scope note is what permits it here.
242	
243	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same prose input in a non-final position:**
244	
245	```text
246	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + C2's threshold + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown)
247	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
248	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
249	```
250	
251	This head breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with a well-formed input still to its right the check matches from `GT-12?` onward and never reaches `C2's threshold`. Write `C2 (threshold)` wherever the input sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
252	
253	**Non-conforming — a hop beginning with a GT-N identifier:**
254	
255	```text
256	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
257	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
258	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
259	```
260

120	## Scoring Model
121	
122	Score each of the 6 criteria using this shared 4-level scale, applied uniformly across all criteria
123	(highest to lowest):
124	
125	- **Rigorous** — the criterion's named artifact is present, structurally complete, and every
126	  entry meets the observable descriptor for this level: all required fields are populated with
127	  non-generic content, all required relationships are explicit,
128	  and every observable structural test in this criterion's Rigorous descriptor returns pass.
129	
130	- **Sound** — the criterion's named artifact is present and mostly meets the Rigorous descriptor,
131	  but one or more entries fall short in a specific, identifiable way: a field is generic or vague
132	  rather than empty, a relationship is implicit rather than absent, or one entry departs from the
133	  prescribed form without invalidating the rest.
134	
135	- **Hand-wavy** — the criterion's named artifact is present but fails the Rigorous descriptor in
136	  a pattern rather than an isolated entry: multiple fields are generic or empty, the artifact's
137	  prescribed structure is not followed, or the section uses the honest-depth escape valve with a
138	  reason that could be copy-pasted to any analysis without modification.
139	
140	- **Absent** — the criterion's named artifact is missing entirely, or the section exists but
141	  contains no content that could be scored against the artifact's descriptor (the section heading
142	  appears with nothing substantive below it).
143	
144	**Rank order (explicit):** Rigorous > Sound > Hand-wavy > Absent.
145	
146	**Gate:** Any criterion scored **Absent** fails the entire analysis — it must be revised and
147	re-scored, bounded to at most one re-perception pass per analysis, per "How to Apply This
148	Gate" above. If the criterion still scores Absent after that single pass, it is presented as
149	an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being withheld, regardless of how
150	all other criteria score.
151	
152	**Hand-wavy cap:** Two or more criteria scored **Hand-wavy** also fails the entire analysis —
153	the same bound applies: revise and re-score once, per "How to Apply This Gate" above. One
154	criterion at Hand-wavy is tolerated (one isolated weaker section does not indicate a systemic
155	quality problem); two or more at Hand-wavy indicates a pattern of shallow reasoning that the
156	gate alone cannot catch, because no single criterion has reached the gate-fail level. If two or
157	more criteria still score Hand-wavy after that single pass, the cap breach is presented as an
158	unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being withheld.
159	
160	**Pass:** No criterion scores Absent, and at most one criterion scores Hand-wavy.
161	(Equivalently: every criterion is Sound or above, except at most one may be Hand-wavy.)
162	
163	**Escape-valve scoring (global rule, applies to every criterion):** Any section that
164	legitimately uses the honest-depth escape valve (`Nothing material here — [reason]`) is
165	scored **Rigorous** if the stated reason is specific to this analysis — it names a property
166	of this problem that makes the section's content unnecessary — and **Hand-wavy** if the
167	reason is generic or copy-pasteable to any analysis. A properly-used escape valve is
168	**never** scored Absent solely for using the escape valve: the per-criterion Absent
169	descriptors below apply to a section that is missing, empty, or filled with non-scoreable
170	content, not to a section that is honestly and specifically marked as having no material
171	content.
172	
173	**Load-bearing chain (definition):** A derivation chain is *load-bearing* if a claim in
174	the Conclusion section (output section 6) depends on it — i.e., the chain produces, or is
175	cited as support for, a conclusion the analysis actually presents. A chain that reaches
176	only an intermediate result no conclusion rests on is not load-bearing. (This is the
177	narrower scoring sense of the phrase `SKILL.md` uses informally as "load-bearing for a
178	high-stakes conclusion.")

## Sadasivan's Theoretical Impossibility Result

Sadasivan et al. (2023) posit theoretical arguments stating that when there is a strong overlap between machine and human-generated text distributions, it is impossible to detect AI-generated text.

More specifically, they provide a theoretical impossibility result indicating that as language models become more sophisticated and better at emulating human text, the performance of even the best-possible detector decreases. For a sufficiently advanced language model seeking to imitate human text, even the best-possible detector may only perform marginally better than a random classifier.

## Empirical Findings

Beyond theory, Sadasivan et al. show that several AI-text detectors are not reliable in practical scenarios, demonstrating that paraphrasing attacks can break a whole range of detectors, including ones using watermarking schemes as well as neural network-based detectors and zero-shot classifiers.

## Counterarguments

However, the impossibility claim has faced criticism. Chakraborty et al. (2023) argue that the impossibility results posited by Sadasivan et al. could be conservative in practical scenarios, noting that the impossibility result does not consider the potential number of text sequences available or the length of the text sequence, which can impact the detectability significantly. Chakraborty et al. derive a precise sample complexity analysis and show that it is almost always possible to detect AI-generated text from information-theoretic principles if one can collect enough samples or increase the sequence length.

Based on the search results, I can provide you with comprehensive information about Messick's construct validity and construct-irrelevant variance in educational measurement:

## Construct Validity

Construct validity is the extent to which an instrument actually measures the theoretical construct it claims to measure. Following Messick (1989), construct validity is now treated as the superordinate validity concept, where all validity evidence — whether from test content, criterion correlations, or consequence analysis — constitutes evidence about construct validity interpretation.

## Construct-Irrelevant Variance

Construct irrelevant test variance is the extent to which test scores are influenced by factors that are irrelevant to the construct that the test is intended to measure. More specifically, construct-irrelevant variance is when a test captures systematic variance unrelated to the construct — such as reading load on a maths test — distorting scores for reasons external to the attribute being measured.

### Forms of Construct-Irrelevant Variance

Construct irrelevant variance may arise in two forms: construct-irrelevant easiness and construct-irrelevant difficulty, with construct-irrelevant difficulty resulting in invalidly low scores and construct-irrelevant easiness lessening the difficulty of the test. Construct-irrelevant easy items include items that are susceptible to 'test-wise' solutions, giving an advantage to 'test-wise' examinees who obtain scores which are invalidly high for them.

## Threats to Validity

There are two main threats to validity: construct under representation, which is the extent to which a test fails to capture important aspects of the construct the test is intended to measure, and construct irrelevant test variance.

# Construct-Irrelevant Variance in Messick's Framework

Based on the article, the definition of construct-irrelevant variance (CIV) comes from Messick's work on validity. The article states:

"any bias that results in systematic higher or lower scores is CIV" (following the Standards, AERA & NCME, 2014, which extended Messick's original framework).

## Distinguishing Valid from Contaminated Measures

The article emphasizes that a valid assessment should have scores primarily reflecting the **construct of interest (COI)**—the intended skill or knowledge being measured. In contrast, contaminated measures include CIV, which are unintended sources of systematic error that do not represent the actual competency being assessed.

As the article explains, contextual features in assessments "that engage and motivate one examinee and facilitate his or her effective task performances may alienate and confuse another examinee and bias or distort task performance." This distinction reveals how rich assessment contexts can either enhance validity by creating authentic scenarios or compromise it by introducing construct-irrelevant factors that artificially inflate or deflate scores independent of actual skill.

# First-Principles Analysis: Should a University Replace Timed Exams with Take-Home Assessments Given Widely Available AI Writing Assistants?

*Mode: full-composer (no single-technique trigger fired; all eight companion techniques applied — five-whys, fishbone, inversion, pre-mortem, trade-off, second-order thinking, estimate, theoretical-limit). Reference files opened this session: `output-template.md` and `validation-rubric.md` (both read successfully, in full, before assembly).*

---

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** Whether a university should adopt a uniform policy of replacing timed written exams with take-home assessments in response to widely available AI writing assistants, or whether the soundness of any given assessment format is instead conditional on *which competency (construct) that specific assessment is designed to certify* — making "replace" potentially the wrong question to ask at all.

**Success criteria** (each independently checkable against Section 6 below):
- **SC1:** Section 6 states, for at least two distinct construct categories (e.g., unaided recall/argumentation vs. tool-mediated synthesis/applied work), which assessment format(s) are recommended for that category.
- **SC2:** Section 6 explicitly accepts or rejects "replace" as the correct decision frame, naming the alternative frame if rejected.
- **SC3:** Section 6 names at least one specific enforcement mechanism it recommends *against*, together with the ground truth that rules it out.
- **SC4:** Section 6 names at least one second-order risk of its own recommendation and a corresponding mitigation.
- **SC5:** This analysis states an explicit falsification condition for the recommendation (recorded in the adversarial pass record below, per the methodology's rule that falsification conditions live there, not in §6).

---

## 2. Assumptions Table

**Fishbone (cause-category brainstorm feeding this table).** The assumption space here is multi-causal, so I brainstormed across the default six categories before classifying:

- *People* — student incentive to save effort; faculty inertia/AI-literacy gaps; administrators' reputational risk-aversion.
- *Process* — assignment design (generic vs. personalized prompts); rubric focus (product vs. process); appeals/due-process burden.
- *Technology & Tools* — LLM cost/availability; detector unreliability; process-logging tools (draft history) availability.
- *Environment* — accreditation requirements; inter-institutional reputational competition; the labor market's reliance on the credential's signal.
- *Information* — no shared definition of what "AI assistance" even means (spell-check vs. full generation); ambiguity about which construct a given assessment targets.
- *Resources* — faculty redesign time; funding for oral-exam infrastructure; TA support for richer grading.

**Inversion (failure-precondition brainstorm feeding this table).** Inverting the question's literal claim ("a university should replace timed exams with take-home assessments"), I enumerated conditions that would guarantee this policy fails, then derived the necessary preconditions those conditions expose (rows A11, A12 below; A13–A17 were surfaced later, during the Phase 4 Assumption Audit, and are added to this same table per the methodology).

| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1: Take-home is "newly vulnerable" to AI while timed exams are "not" (blanket claim) | untested belief | verify or flag | Challenge — overgeneralized; true for the writing-generation vector, false for take-home types that don't reduce to prose (novel-data analysis, code with test suites, oral components), and ignores exams' own pre-existing integrity gaps | unverified — flagged; addressed by GT-5/GT-6 |
| A2: AI-text detectors can reliably distinguish AI from human writing, now or with foreseeable improvement | untested belief | verify or flag | Discard — contradicted by GT-1 and GT-2 | GT-1, GT-2 (read-at-source) |
| A3: Assessment's primary/sole purpose is integrity certification | convention | challenge before use | Challenge — assessment also serves formative feedback, motivation, and ranking; optimizing purely for anti-AI robustness trades off against these | unverified — flagged (standard assessment-purposes literature, not opened this session) |
| A4: University assessment policy is or should be one uniform binary choice | convention | challenge before use | Discard — institutions already differentiate by course/level/discipline; uniformity is an administrative convenience, not a requirement | definitional — self-evidently differentiable in principle |
| A5: Take-home favors resourced students, therefore is *less equitable* than timed exams | untested belief | verify or flag | Challenge — incomplete; timed exams carry their own equity costs (test anxiety, disability-accommodation friction, second-language processing speed under time pressure); net comparison is context-dependent, not unidirectional | unverified — flagged |
| A6/GT-7: AI writing assistants producing fluent academic-register prose on demand are, as of 2026, cheaply/freely available to typical students | current constraint | record expiry | Accept — expires only if access is restricted or capability regresses; neither is a realistic near-term expectation | unverified — flagged (stipulated by the question's own premise; no specific access/pricing source opened this session) |
| A7: Take-home's unverifiability is a permanent, unfixable state | untested belief | verify or flag | Challenge — false as a blanket claim; verification-by-design (oral defense, personalized/novel data, process/version-history capture) exists today | GT-6 (definitional); chain C4 |
| A8: "Writing" is one undifferentiated construct across all assessments | convention | challenge before use | Discard — construct varies (recall vs. argumentation vs. craft vs. applied problem-solving vs. research synthesis); AI's threat depends on which construct is at stake | GT-4 |
| A9: Faculty grading/redesign capacity is unlimited or irrelevant to the choice | current constraint | record expiry | Accept, with expiry — expires with added TA/funding investment; until then, feasibility must be scored explicitly | reflected in C3's feasibility score |
| A10: Student behavior/incentives are unaffected by format/enforcement choice | untested belief | verify or flag | Discard as a simplifying assumption — second-order analysis (C4) shows incentive effects are real and load-bearing | chain C4 |
| A11: The construct being certified can be adequately verified without confirming who produced the artifact | untested belief | verify or flag | Discard for constructs where individual authorship *is* the credential claim (licensure-adjacent, foundational gatekeeping) | GT-6 |
| A12: One assessment format fits all disciplines/constructs | convention | challenge before use | Discard — format-construct mismatch is a validity problem independent of AI; AI raises the stakes, doesn't create the issue | chain C1 |
| A13 *(surfaced, C1 hop 3)*: Tool-mediated synthesis/iterative work is authentic to real disciplinary practice in at least some fields | untested belief | verify or flag | Accept, provisionally — plausible (mirrors how professionals actually work) but not independently sourced this session | unverified — flagged |
| A14 *(surfaced, C3 hop 1)*: External certifying bodies value verified individual authorship for at least some specific credential claims | untested belief | verify or flag | Accept, provisionally — near-definitional for licensure-type credentials specifically | unverified — flagged |
| A15 *(surfaced, C3 hop 3)*: The trade-off's criteria weights reflect this analysis's judgment, not a measured stakeholder survey | untested belief (methodological) | verify or flag | Accept, with caveat — residual risk is bounded, not eliminated, by the flip-test result in C3 | flip-test computation, chain C3 |
| A16 *(surfaced, C4 hop 2)*: Oral verification components carry nonzero accent/anxiety-related bias risk absent standardized rubrics | untested belief | verify or flag | Accept — consistent with general rater-bias concerns in unstructured oral assessment | unverified — flagged; mitigation in adversarial-pass Cluster 2 |
| A17 *(surfaced, C4 hop 3)*: Live, real-time AI-assisted evasion of oral-defense verification is not yet a practical, widespread threat | untested belief | verify or flag | Accept, provisionally, with explicit expiry condition — the single most time-sensitive input in this analysis | unverified — flagged; monitored per Falsification condition below |

---

## 3. Ground Truths

**Five-Whys (reduce-to-primitives), testing GT-5's irreducibility.** Claim tested: "timed, invigilated exams are AI-proof." Decomposed: (a) no internet/device access during the exam [procedural, verifiable]; (b) no external human assistance during the exam [procedural, verifiable]; (c) content produced in the window is authored by the candidate [follows from (a)+(b) *if enforced*]; (d) enforcement of (a)/(b) is actually effective in every instance [empirical, **not** verified — invigilation quality varies; impersonation and exam leaks are known, pre-existing failure modes]. **Verdict: the claim does not bottom out at a physical law — it bottoms out at "conditional on competently executed invigilation."** GT-5 below is phrased accordingly, and this finding becomes a live rival addressed in the adversarial pass (Section 5 / below).

**Provenance summary:** `?`-marked: GT-3, GT-7 (2 of 7). Read-at-source: GT-1 — arXiv:2304.02819, results section, quoted "average false positive rate: 61.22%" and "89 of the 91... (97.80%)... flagged"; GT-2 — arXiv:2303.11156, abstract, quoted "theoretical framework connecting the AUROC of the best possible detector to the Total Variation distance..." and "our recursive paraphrasing method can significantly reduce detection rates"; GT-4 — Frontiers in Education (2021), quoted "any bias that results in systematic higher or lower scores is CIV."

- **GT-1** Across seven widely used AI-text detectors (Originality.AI, Quil.org, Sapling, OpenAI's classifier, Crossplag, GPTZero, ZeroGPT) tested on 91 TOEFL essays written by non-native English speakers, the average false-positive rate was 61.22%, with 97.80% of essays flagged by at least one detector — versus near-perfect accuracy on a native-English-speaker control set. — source: Liang, Yuksekgonul, Mao, Wu & Zou, *Patterns* (2023) / arXiv:2304.02819; read-at-source: results section, fetched directly this session.
- **GT-2** The best achievable accuracy (AUROC) of *any* AI-text detector is mathematically bounded by the total-variation distance between human-text and AI-text distributions — a distance that shrinks as language models improve — and a recursive paraphrasing attack already significantly reduces detection rates across watermarking-based, neural-network-based, zero-shot, and retrieval-based detectors. — source: Sadasivan, Kumar, Balasubramanian, Wang & Feizi, arXiv:2303.11156 (2023); read-at-source: abstract, fetched directly this session.
- **GT-3?** Unauthorized-assistance use in assignment-style work substantially predates generative AI: a systematic review found reported contract-cheating rates rising from an average 3.52% (studies since 1978) to 15.7% (studies since 2014), and a UK QAA-cited estimate suggests roughly one in seven graduates may have paid someone to complete an assignment. — cited to: systematic review / QAA report, surfaced via search; **Phase 3 failure record:** attempted to open the primary article (tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14703297.2023.2190148) via WebFetch; server returned HTTP 403 Forbidden (paywalled) — source unreachable. Remains reported-by-delegate/unverified; used only in a MEDIUM/LOW-confidence supporting role, never as sole support for a HIGH claim.
- **GT-4** Educational-measurement validity theory (Messick's construct-validity framework, as extended in the AERA/APA/NCME *Standards*) defines construct-irrelevant variance as systematic score variance from factors unrelated to the intended construct, including "construct-irrelevant easiness" — score inflation from factors unrelated to the competency being measured. — source: "A Framework of Construct-Irrelevant Variance for Contextualized Constructed Response Assessment," *Frontiers in Education* (2021); read-at-source: definitional passage, fetched directly this session.
- **GT-5** A timed, invigilated, closed-book, no-device exam prevents, by construction of the modality — continuous observation, no internet/device access, fixed time window — a candidate from delegating real-time authorship of the specific exam response to another agent, **conditional on the invigilation protocol being competently executed** (per the five-whys finding above; not an absolute guarantee). — source: definitional, given standard invigilation protocol.
- **GT-6** A take-home assessment administered without proctoring, device restriction, or real-time monitoring cannot, from the submitted artifact alone, distinguish unaided authorship from AI-assisted or ghost-written authorship, absent an added independent verification mechanism (oral defense, personalized/novel data the model could not have prior access to, or process/version-history capture). — source: definitional, logical complement of GT-5.
- **GT-7?** AI writing assistants capable of producing fluent, structurally competent academic-register prose on demand are, as of 2026, cheaply or freely available to typical students. — unverified: stipulated by the question's own premise; no specific access/pricing source opened this session.

---

## 4. Derivation Chains

**Theoretical-limit application (feeding C2).** Governing constraint: information-theoretic distinguishability between human and AI text, per GT-2. Ideal ceiling: as language models improve, the total-variation distance between the two distributions shrinks toward zero, so the best-possible detector's achievable accuracy is bounded above by a quantity that *falls* toward chance-level as capability rises — an unusual theoretical-limit case where the ceiling itself degrades over time rather than offering headroom. Best demonstrated: today's detectors already sit far below even a naive expectation of reliability (GT-1's 61.22% false-positive rate against non-native writers). Conventional figure: institutional policy documents typically treat detector output as if it were a reliable signal. Gap 1 (conventional → best-demonstrated): already large and *currently existing*, not a future risk. Gap 2 (best-demonstrated → ideal ceiling): small and shrinking — there is little to no headroom for "just build a better detector," because the ceiling is falling to meet or fall below current unreliable performance. This is the key finding that makes "don't rely on detection" an institutionally *permanent* conclusion rather than a statement about current software immaturity.

**Estimate (Fermi) application (feeding C2).** Target quantity: false cheating-accusation incidents per year at a representative mid-size university if AI detectors were used as a primary check on take-home writing. Unit factors: non-native-English-speaking enrollment (~1,000–2,000 students, order-of-magnitude assumption) × fraction submitting checked writing (~0.5–1.0) × false-positive rate (GT-1: 0.30–0.85 range across detectors, 0.61 central). Central estimate: 1,500 × 0.80 × 0.61 ≈ 730/year. Bracket: **[150, 730, 1,700] false-flag incidents/year at one institution.** Decision-resolution check: both ends of the bracket support the same conclusion (detector-based enforcement is operationally and ethically unmanageable even under conservative assumptions), so the estimate is resolved without needing tighter inputs.

### Conclusion C1: AI assistance is a construct-conditional threat, not a format-conditional one — and it intensifies a pre-existing problem rather than creating a new one

GT-3? (contract cheating predates AI) + GT-4 (construct-irrelevant variance) + GT-7? (AI assistants widely available)
→ unauthorized-authorship risk in assignment-style work already existed at meaningful scale before generative AI, so AI does not introduce a wholly new failure mode — it changes the cost, speed, and per-instance undetectability of an existing one
→ because AI can now supply fluent, structurally competent prose on demand at near-zero cost, any assessment whose intended construct is "the enrolled student's own unaided production of that prose" now admits a far larger, more systematic source of unintended score inflation than contract cheating alone provided — textbook construct-irrelevant easiness
→ where the intended construct is instead synthesizing a specific novel dataset the model has not seen, defending reasoning live under follow-up questioning, or executing a multi-step technical procedure checked independently of prose quality, AI assistance does not inflate the score the same way, and may be authentic to real disciplinary practice *[Assumes: A13 — tool-mediated synthesis is authentic to practice in at least some fields; if false, this hop's motivating rationale weakens, but the tier-2 case survives on GT-4's construct-definition alone, so the endpoint still stands]*
→ therefore whether AI assistance threatens validity is a property of the construct an assessment certifies, magnified in scale by AI but not created by it, not a property of "take-home" versus "timed" as such

**Pre-check:** head GT-3?, GT-4, GT-7? · ?-marked: GT-3?, GT-7? · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — Inputs axis short on GT-3? and GT-7?; verification that would remove GT-3? is opening the paywalled source or an open-access equivalent, and for GT-7?, citing a specific dated access/pricing figure. The rival "AI assistance always inflates scores regardless of construct" is not left open here — it is resolved by this analysis's own tiered conclusion (chain C5), which includes a no-tools-baseline tier rather than treating tiers as mutually exclusive.

### Conclusion C2: AI-text detection cannot serve as a reliable, durable integrity control for take-home work

GT-1 (61.22% detector false-positive rate, non-native writers) + GT-2 (theoretical detection ceiling degrades with model capability)
→ detectors already misclassify genuine human writing at a rate high enough, and biased enough against a specific population, to make detector output an unreliable signal today
→ the achievable ceiling on any detector's accuracy is mathematically bounded by how distinguishable AI text is from human text, a distance that provably shrinks as models improve, while simple paraphrasing already defeats current detectors including watermarking-based ones
→ therefore detection reliability will not improve enough to fix today's unreliability, and will plausibly degrade further, so "add better detection software" is not a viable long-term integrity strategy, independent of institutional resourcing

**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-2 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** HIGH — both inputs are read-at-source with named locations; each hop follows by cited regularity; the rival "better detectors are coming" is ruled out by GT-2's theoretical bound itself, which is a stronger claim than an engineering-maturity gap.

### Conclusion C3: A construct-conditional hybrid/portfolio policy dominates a uniform swap in either direction

C1 (MEDIUM: construct-conditional threat) + C2 (HIGH: detection unreliable) + GT-6 (take-home w/o verification can't confirm authorship)
→ because detection cannot be relied upon and take-home without added verification structurally cannot confirm authorship, a uniform "replace timed exams with take-home" policy fails to certify individual-authorship constructs to external parties *[Assumes: A14 — external certifying bodies value verified authorship for at least some credential claims]* and is eliminated as a general policy, not merely disfavored
→ because whether AI assistance threatens validity depends on the construct, a uniform "keep timed exams for everything" policy also mismatches format to construct wherever tool-mediated synthesis or applied problem-solving is the actual competency being certified
→ a weighted trade-off across six decision criteria (construct fit, certification reliability, equity, feasibility, formative feedback, resilience to future AI capability) scores uniform-timed-exam at 79 and construct-conditional-hybrid at 94 — a gap no single criterion's reweighting closes within the standard 1–5 weighting scale *[Assumes: A15 — the weights reflect analyst judgment, not a surveyed consensus; priced by the flip-test below]*

**Trade-off table (must-haves as knockouts, then weighted scoring):**

| Must-have | A: uniform timed exam | B: uniform take-home | C: construct-conditional hybrid |
|---|---|---|---|
| MH1: Does not rely on unreliable AI detection as enforcement backbone | pass | **fails** (as commonly implemented, per GT-1/GT-2) | pass |
| MH2: Can certify individual-authorship constructs to external parties | pass | **fails** for that construct subset, absent added verification | pass |
| MH3: Operationally feasible at typical staffing | pass | pass | pass, *if scoped/selective* |

*B is eliminated, not merely scored low.* Remaining comparison, A vs. C (weights in parentheses; anchors: 1=worst, 5=best on each criterion):

| Criterion (weight) | A score | C score |
|---|---|---|
| Construct fit (5) | 2 | 5 |
| Certification reliability (5) | 4 | 4 |
| Equity, net both directions (4) | 2 | 3 |
| Feasibility/workload (3) | 5 | 3 |
| Feedback/motivation (3) | 2 | 4 |
| Resilience to future AI capability (4) | 5 | 4 |
| **Weighted total** | **79** | **94** |

**Flip test:** the largest single-criterion swing available within the 1–5 weight scale (moving construct-fit's weight from 5 to its floor of 1) still leaves C ahead (94−12=82 vs. 79 unchanged is not quite right — recomputed: reducing that weight's contribution by 12 points brings the gap from 15 to 3; C still wins). No single-criterion reweighting within the standard scale flips the winner to A. **This is the strongest result the trade-off procedure can return.**

**Pre-check:** head C1 (MEDIUM), C2 (HIGH), GT-6 · ?-marked: none directly · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — capped by C1's MEDIUM rating (itself caused by GT-3?/GT-7? provenance gaps, not by any weakness in the trade-off arithmetic itself, which recomputes cleanly and is robust to reweighting per the flip test).

### Conclusion C4: Responsible implementation requires scoping, standardized verification rubrics, and monitoring — and is durable but not permanent

C3 (MEDIUM: hybrid dominates)
→ [2nd-order, actor lens] faculty asked to add individualized verification to every assessment in every course face a workload increase that is only net-positive if scoped selectively (spot-checks, not universal per-artifact oral defense), per C3's feasibility score
→ [2nd-order, actor lens] students facing oral-defense components may experience differential accent-, anxiety-, or language-related grading bias absent standardized rubrics and structured questioning protocols *[Assumes: A16 — oral verification carries nonzero bias risk absent standardization]*
→ [2nd-order, time lens] shared item banks and standardized rubrics reduce the initial workload spike over several terms, but a longer-horizon risk remains that sufficiently fluent, low-latency conversational AI could eventually assist even live oral defenses *[Assumes: A17 — live AI-assisted oral-defense evasion is not yet a practical, widespread threat; if false, this specific verification mechanism weakens, though the broader construct-conditional framing in C1/C3 does not]*

**Pre-check:** head C3 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: none directly · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** LOW — two axes are short: (1) Inputs, inherited from C3's MEDIUM cap; (2) Inference, because the third hop rests on A17, an explicitly unpriced premise whose failure would weaken the specific oral-defense mechanism this chain recommends (not the broader tiering). No evidence available to this analysis settles A17's timeline; the Falsification condition in the adversarial pass record below names the observation that would require revisiting it.

### Conclusion C5: Recommended policy — a construct-conditional, tiered assessment portfolio

C3 (MEDIUM: hybrid dominates uniform swap) + C4 (LOW: scoped/monitored implementation)
→ given that detection-based enforcement is not viable and format-vulnerability is construct-dependent (C3), and that responsible implementation requires scoped, phased, bias-mitigated rollout (C4), the defensible institutional default is a tiered portfolio rather than a single format
→ tier 1 — for constructs whose credential claim is "this individual can do X unaided" (foundational-competency checkpoints, licensure-adjacent courses, prerequisite gatekeeping): retain or expand timed/invigilated or otherwise directly-verified (in-class, oral) assessment, accepting its own residual, historically-known imperfections (impersonation/leak risk, per the five-whys finding on GT-5) as a smaller, more manageable risk than unverifiable take-home
→ tier 2 — for constructs whose credential claim includes tool-mediated synthesis, iterative revision, or applied multi-step work with personalized/novel data: permit and design for take-home and AI-tool use, with authorship/competence verified via oral-defense spot-checks, personalized data the model cannot have memorized, or process/version-history capture — never via AI-text detectors

**Pre-check:** head C3 (MEDIUM), C4 (LOW) · ?-marked: none directly · lowest cited: LOW · Inputs ceiling: LOW
**Confidence:** LOW — the core claim (construct-conditional tiering dominates a uniform binary swap) rests on C3 (MEDIUM). The overall band is governed by C4 (LOW), which carries the implementation-scoping and bias-mitigation portion of this recommendation and rests on the explicitly unpriced A17. This is a calibrated LOW, not an under-argued one: the recommendation's *direction* is more robust than its *durability claim* about oral verification specifically.

---

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Mandate AI-detection software as the primary integrity control for take-home work

**What was tried:** Treating unreliable detectors as a solvable engineering-maturity problem — "require Turnitin/GPTZero-style checks on all submissions."
**Why abandoned:** Contradicted by GT-1 (severe, population-biased false-positive rate) and GT-2 (a theoretical, not merely empirical, ceiling that degrades as models improve; paraphrasing already defeats current detectors).
**What it ruled out:** Saves future analysts from re-proposing detection-as-primary-control as if better software could eventually fix it — chain C2 shows the ceiling falls, not rises, with model capability.

### Dead End: Revert entirely to timed, invigilated exams for everything

**What was tried:** Treating Option A as a costless, fully solved default because it is structurally AI-proof.
**Why abandoned:** Fails the trade-off's construct-fit and feedback/motivation criteria for constructs where tool-mediated synthesis is authentic to the discipline (C1, C3); the five-whys decomposition of GT-5 also shows invigilation is "AI-proof" only conditional on competent execution — impersonation and exam leaks are known, non-eliminated failure modes, so treating exams as *perfectly* secure overclaims even the strongest case for uniform A.
**What it ruled out:** Saves future analysts from treating "just go back to blue books" as a complete, risk-free answer.

### Dead End: Resolve the equity question in the abstract ("which format is more equitable, full stop")

**What was tried:** Seeking a single, institution-independent verdict on whether take-home or timed exams are "more equitable."
**Why abandoned:** Equity costs run in both directions (A5) and are not commensurable without specifying which students and which accommodation infrastructure a given institution already has; a context-free verdict is not supportable.
**What it ruled out:** Saves future analysts from expecting this analysis (or any analysis at this level of generality) to resolve equity by fiat rather than by institution-specific design choices named in C4's disposition.

*Note: the rival claim "AI assistance always inflates scores regardless of construct, since even tool-authentic constructs need a demonstrated no-tools baseline first" is intentionally **not** listed here as abandoned — it remains live and is explicitly addressed (not eliminated) by C5's tiered structure, which supplies exactly such a no-tools baseline tier without requiring every assessment to be tools-free.*

---

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Adopt a construct-conditional, tiered assessment portfolio rather than a uniform swap in either direction: retain or expand timed, invigilated, or otherwise directly-verified assessment (in-class writing, oral checkpoints) for constructs whose credential claim is that a specific individual can perform unaided — foundational-competency gatekeeping and licensure-adjacent coursework — and permit, and even design for, take-home and AI-tool-inclusive assessment for constructs where tool-mediated synthesis or iterative applied work is authentic to the discipline, provided authorship/competence is verified by means other than AI-text detection — oral-defense spot-checks, personalized or novel data the model could not have memorized, or process/version-history capture (chain C3).

**Key insight:** The AI-detectability gap the question poses is a proxy for the real variable, which is what construct a given assessment is meant to certify. AI assistance is a validity-destroying "construct-irrelevant easiness" only for assessments whose construct is unaided individual production; it is not necessarily even a threat for assessments whose construct includes tool-mediated work. Meanwhile, reverting to timed exams for everything would itself be a format-construct mismatch for the latter category, and the seemingly obvious fix for the former — better AI detectors — is ruled out not by current software immaturity but by a theoretical bound that gets *worse*, not better, as models improve (chain C1; chain C2).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** This recommendation forgoes the administrative simplicity of one uniform rule, accepts real transition costs (faculty redesign time, standardized rubric development for oral components, a multi-term implementation runway), and accepts an unresolved, monitored risk that live, real-time AI assistance could eventually erode oral-defense verification the way static-text generation eroded take-home writing (chain C4).

## 4. Derivation Chains

**Theoretical-limit application (feeding C2).** Governing constraint: information-theoretic distinguishability between human and AI text, per GT-2. Ideal ceiling: as language models improve, the total-variation distance between the two distributions shrinks toward zero, so the best-possible detector's achievable accuracy is bounded above by a quantity that *falls* toward chance-level as capability rises — an unusual theoretical-limit case where the ceiling itself degrades over time rather than offering headroom. Best demonstrated: today's detectors already sit far below even a naive expectation of reliability (GT-1's 61.22% false-positive rate against non-native writers). Conventional figure: institutional policy documents typically treat detector output as if it were a reliable signal. Gap 1 (conventional → best-demonstrated): already large and *currently existing*, not a future risk. Gap 2 (best-demonstrated → ideal ceiling): small and shrinking — there is little to no headroom for "just build a better detector," because the ceiling is falling to meet or fall below current unreliable performance. This is the key finding that makes "don't rely on detection" an institutionally *permanent* conclusion rather than a statement about current software immaturity.

**Estimate (Fermi) application (feeding C2).** Target quantity: false cheating-accusation incidents per year at a representative mid-size university if AI detectors were used as a primary check on take-home writing. **Recommended approach:** Adopt a construct-conditional, tiered assessment portfolio rather than a uniform swap in either direction: retain or expand timed, invigilated, or otherwise directly-verified assessment (in-class writing, oral checkpoints) for constructs whose credential claim is that a specific individual can perform unaided — foundational-competency gatekeeping and licensure-adjacent coursework — and permit, and even design for, take-home and AI-tool-inclusive assessment for constructs where tool-mediated synthesis or iterative applied work is authentic to the discipline, provided authorship/competence is verified by means other than AI-text detection — oral-defense spot-checks, personalized or novel data the model could not have memorized, or process/version-history capture (chain C3).

**Key insight:** The AI-detectability gap the question poses is a proxy for the real variable, which is what construct a given assessment is meant to certify. AI assistance is a validity-destroying "construct-irrelevant easiness" only for assessments whose construct is unaided individual production; it is not necessarily even a threat for assessments whose construct includes tool-mediated work. Meanwhile, reverting to timed exams for everything would itself be a format-construct mismatch for the latter category, and the seemingly obvious fix for the former — better AI detectors — is ruled out not by current software immaturity but by a theoretical bound that gets *worse*, not better, as models improve (chain C1; chain C2).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** This recommendation forgoes the administrative simplicity of one uniform rule, accepts real transition costs (faculty redesign time, standardized rubric development for oral components, a multi-term implementation runway), and accepts an unresolved, monitored risk that live, real-time AI assistance could eventually erode oral-defense verification the way static-text generation eroded take-home writing (chain C4).
